name: result
intent: Make every fallible step return one value that carries either the success payload or the failure reason, so failures travel with the data along a short-circuiting error track instead of unwinding around it as exceptions, sentinels or out-of-band status codes.
problem: Expected, recoverable failures have no place in the signature: an exception named only in prose unwinds past every intermediate caller and can be swallowed on the way, a status code or sentinel return is silently ignored, and a reason flattened into a message string cannot be branched on. The same mistake then repeats - callers forget the error channel, treat a failure as data, or discover a missed case in production - because nothing in the code forces the failure to be seen.
context: Code that composes several fallible steps and whose callers must branch on the outcome: parsing and validation at a boundary, application services mapping domain failures to transport responses, I/O and integrations where not-found, conflict and unavailable must be told apart and retried selectively, and pipelines of transformations. It applies wherever the language can express a two-case value (sum type, sealed hierarchy, discriminated union, stdlib Result-like type) and can chain such values (?/and_then/bind/for-comprehension), and it suits runtimes where exceptions are unavailable, expensive or discouraged - C, Go, embedded, WebAssembly, FFI boundaries.
benefits: The failure is in the type: a caller cannot reach the payload without passing through the constructors, so an unhandled failure is a visible branch - or, with exhaustiveness checking and must-use discipline (Rust #[must_use], lint rules, sealed types), a compiler error instead of a production surprise.

Fallible steps compose along one track: and_then/bind/?/for-comprehension connects steps so the first failure short-circuits the rest while keeping its reason, and the happy path stays a linear chain instead of nested try/if pyramids.

The failure is a domain value: callers branch on structured cases (error enums, sealed variants, sentinels behind errors.Is/errors.As) instead of parsing message strings, and failures can be serialized, counted, mapped to HTTP statuses or retried by policy.
Both branches are ordinary values: tests construct Success and Failure directly and assert on them, with nothing to throw, catch or mock - the failure path is as cheap to exercise as the happy path.

Conversion happens once, at the boundary: exceptions, null returns, sentinel codes and transport errors are translated into Result in one adapter (safe/fromThrowable/runCatching/ok_or_else), so the core stays exception-free and the translation is testable in isolation.

The exit policy is caller-owned and explicit: the terminal handler chooses between defaulting (unwrapOr/orElse), translating, retrying or propagating, keeping the decision where the context is instead of forcing a producer-side fallback.

Works where exceptions cannot: in C, Go, embedded and cross-language boundaries the pattern names the convention that error-carrying returns already follow, and it lets a library expose failures without imposing an exception type on its callers.
tradeoffs: Wrapper contagion: every function along the path changes its signature to Result, so retrofitting the pattern into existing code is a breaking change through the whole call tree - exceptions, by contrast, propagate without touching intermediate signatures.

Ceremony without sugar: the pattern pays off only where the language or a library provides composition; without ?/and_then/bind/for-comprehensions the happy path turns into nested matches and the error handling doubles the code it was meant to protect.

Two error channels coexist: exceptions remain correct for programmer errors and genuinely exceptional technical faults, so every boundary between throw and Result is a conversion point - and mixing them carelessly (catch, log, continue) silently swallows failures.

Error-type design debt: String failures defeat branching, while one god error enum shared by every layer leaks implementation details across boundaries; the failure type is an API contract and must be designed like one.

The railway hides control flow: readers must know the combinators to follow a chain, and diagnosing where a Failure originated requires deliberately attached context (map_err/context()/with_context); otherwise the terminal error says only that something failed.

Representation and allocation cost: each step wraps a value; garbage-collected languages pay an allocation per step, Rust and Swift niche optimizations cover only specific layouts, and a large failure payload inflates every return value.

Accumulation is opt-in and surprises: the default is fail-fast, so a caller who needs every validation error must consciously switch to an accumulating form (Validated/combineWithAllErrors) - otherwise the first error silently hides all the rest.

participants.responsibility: Carries the value produced when a step succeeds; it is built only through the type's success constructor, so it can never be confused with the failure case.
Carries the reason a step failed as a domain value (error enum, sealed variant, sentinel, exception kept as data), so callers can branch, translate, retry or render it without parsing text.
Returns the two-case value instead of throwing or returning a sentinel, states the possibility of failure in its signature, and never invents a default for a failure it cannot resolve.

participants.role: Combinator / railway (and_then, bind, ?, for-comprehension, map, map_err)
participants.responsibility: Consumes one result and applies the next fallible step, short-circuiting the failure track unchanged; the mapping combinators adapt one side's payload without leaving the track.

participants.role: Boundary adapter (safe, fromThrowable, runCatching, ok_or_else, Result(catching:))
participants.responsibility: Converts the exception/status-code/null world into the two-case value exactly where the failure originates, so the core logic never throws for expected failures.

participants.role: Terminal handler (match/fold, unwrapOr, orElse, Else, Switch)
participants.responsibility: Consumes the result once and exhaustively: applies the default, renders or translates the failure, retries, or propagates a new result to its own caller.

use_cases: Input validation and parsing chains (parse, then validate, then normalize) where any step may fail and the outermost handler renders the failure; accumulating realizations report every field error at once.
Application and use-case services whose transport layer maps domain failures to status codes, problem documents or process exit codes - the failure must be branchable, not a message string.
Persistence and integration calls that must distinguish not-found, conflict, permission and unavailable and act differently (retry, compensate, return 404).
Retry and fallback policies that need a classification boundary: transient versus permanent is a property of the failure value, not of an exception type tree.
Runtimes without exceptions or where they are undesirable: C libraries, embedded code, WebAssembly, FFI boundaries, and Go services following the (T, error) convention.
Asynchronous pipelines where a rejected promise or future destroys the reason (unwrapped rejection, CompletionException); ResultAsync-style types keep the failure typed across the async boundary.
Batch jobs and migrations that must finish the batch and report which items failed, instead of aborting the whole run on the first exception.
Rust's standard-library std::result::Result<T, E> makes recoverable I/O and parsing failures explicit, and the ? operator propagates Err values without losing their typed cause.
F# Core's Result<'T,'TError> and Result.bind support validation pipelines that return either Ok or Error and pattern-match once at the boundary.
Go's standard-library error values and errors.Is/errors.As provide an explicit, inspectable failure channel for service and integration code without exception-based control flow.
avoid_when: The failure is a bug or a broken invariant (index out of range, null dereference): panic/assert/abort, or an unchecked exception, is simpler and more honest than threading a Result through every signature.
Absence rather than failure is meant: a lookup that may legitimately find nothing belongs to Option/Maybe - a Result would force a reason that does not exist.
A single boundary already renders every failure and no caller branches (one top-level handler around a request or job): exceptions with that one handler are less code and equally safe.
The code path must abort anyway (startup configuration, migration precondition): fail fast is the smaller mechanism, and every additional Result return is ceremony.

The language's native error channel is already a checked, composable value and the team uses it consistently - wrapping it in a bespoke Result type duplicates the mechanism (wrapping Go's (T, error), Swift's typed throws, a C# exception hierarchy) and gives the code base two idioms for one job.
anti_patterns: Result as decoration: calling unwrap/getOrThrow/_unsafeUnwrap immediately after every call, so the failure still crashes - one frame later and with a longer signature.
String failures (Result<T, String>): the reason becomes untypable, callers parse messages, and translation, retry and mapping policies cannot be attached to the failure.
Swallowing: logging the failure and continuing with a default value, which turns a handled error path back into a silent one.
Two channels for one operation (throw on one path, Result on another, a sentinel on a third), so no caller can know what to check.
Result in parameters and fields instead of as a return contract: every consumer pays the wrapper and the failure semantics of inputs stay ambiguous.
Wrapper churn: re-encoding a language's native error value into a bespoke Result type (wrapping Go's (T, error), Swift's throws, C#'s exceptions) and maintaining two idioms for one job.
design_principles: Make the failure explicit in the type: no out-of-band channels (prose-only exceptions, sentinels, errno, out-parameters) for failures the caller is expected to handle.
Compose small fallible steps and short-circuit at the first failure - or accumulate deliberately when the caller needs every reason.
Failure is a domain value: model an error type, keep messages for humans, and keep machine decisions on structured cases.
Consume every result once and exhaustively at the terminal handler; design both cases, not only the happy path.
Convert at boundaries exactly once (exception/status/null into Result) so the core is total over its inputs and the translation is testable.
The caller owns the exit policy (default, translate, retry, propagate); a producer never silently picks a fallback.
best_practices: Return Result for every expected failure of a function; keep exceptions and panics for bugs and exceptional technical faults, and say so in the API documentation.
Prefer a named error enum/type over String, and keep each error type at the layer that can interpret it; translate between layers instead of sharing one god error type.
Keep the happy path linear with the language's composition form (?, and_then, bind, for/yield) and reserve match/fold/Switch/Else for the terminal handler.
Never unwrap in production paths except for invariants provable at that line; provide unwrapOr/orElse/getOrElse exits, and enforce consumption with the compiler or a lint rule.
Attach context as the failure propagates (map_err, context(), with_context, %w) so the terminal handler can render a diagnosable error rather than 'something failed'.
Convert exceptions to Result at the boundary where they are thrown (safe, fromThrowable, runCatching, ok_or_else); a Result-returning core must not throw for control flow.
Decide accumulation deliberately: fail fast by default, and switch to an accumulating combinator only where the user must see all validation errors at once.
sources: F# language reference, Results (Microsoft Learn) - Result<'T,'TError> is defined as Ok/Error, composed with Result.bind, and explicitly tied to Railway-Oriented Programming in the F# community; the validateRequest example chains validation steps and forces pattern matching at the end (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fsharp/language-reference/results).

Scott Wlaschin, Railway Oriented Programming - the canonical two-track description: step functions with Success/Failure outputs wired so that a Failure bypasses the remaining steps, connected like railway switches onto a failure track (https://swlaschin.gitbooks.io/fsharpforfunandprofit/content/posts/recipe-part2.html).

Rust standard library, std::result - Result<T, E> as the type for returning and propagating recoverable errors, with the Ok/Err constructors, #[must_use] so an ignored result warns, and the ? operator replacing match-based early returns (https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/index.html).

cppreference, std::expected (C++23) - the C++ vocabulary type for an expected or an unexpected value, with the monadic operations and_then, transform, transform_error and or_else plus the observers has_value/value_or/error() (https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/expected).

Rust standard library Result reference - the canonical Ok(T)/Err(E) vocabulary type, combinators, and ? propagation for recoverable errors (https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/result/enum.Result.html).

FSharp.Core Result module - the official Result.bind and mapping operations used to compose Result<'T,'TError> workflows (https://fsharp.github.io/fsharp-core-docs/reference/fsharp-core-resultmodule.html).
Go blog, Errors are values - standard-library examples of treating errors as explicit values and composing them at service boundaries (https://go.dev/blog/errors-are-values).

Scott Wlaschin, Against Railway-Oriented Programming - a focused criticism that Result/ROP should model expected domain failures rather than replace exceptions for every fault (https://fsharpforfunandprofit.com/posts/against-railway-oriented-programming/).
